title: Seven days
hook: Maya dies a week after the birth; her sister Mahapajapati raises him as her own

segments.voice: Yesterday: the old sage weeps. Asita held the baby and cried because he'd never hear him teach. Your line was plant it anyway. What did you plant? Day twenty-five.
screen: `THE OLD SAGE WEEPS — PLANT IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: So far the story has been all wonders. A shining elephant in a dream. A branch bending down to a queen's hand. Gods cheering in the sky. An old sage weeping over a cradle. It reads like a fairy tale. And then, one week in, the story does something fairy tales usually don't. It turns hard. Seven days after the birth, Queen Maya dies. The baby who everyone says will change the world is one week old, and he has no mother.
screen: `WONDERS, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` → `THEN, ONE WEEK IN.` → `THE BABY HAS NO MOTHER.`

segments.voice: A discourse says it plainly, as if it were simply part of the pattern. Seven days after a future buddha is born, his mother dies. No long scene. The same discourse adds one line: she reappears in a heaven, the Tusita heaven. A later story tells of the Buddha, years afterward, going to teach her among the gods. But on earth, a newborn has lost his mother. And here's who steps in. Maya's younger sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. She's also married to King Suddhodana. She has a baby of her own, a son, Nanda. And the commentaries say she gives her own son to nurses, and nurses Siddhattha herself. She raises him as her own. Years later, it's remembered out loud. In one discourse, Mahapajapati brings the Buddha a gift of new cloth, and his attendant Ananda speaks up for her. She was his mother's sister, Ananda says, his nurse, his foster mother. She nursed him when his own mother died. The discourse keeps that line: a debt of care, said in front of everyone. And Mahapajapati's own story doesn't end there. She'll come back later on this path, with a story of her own. But today is just about this: a child whose first great loss came before he could remember it, and a woman who chose to love him as if he were hers. The tradition keeps them both. The mother who carried him. And the mother who raised him.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AFTER THE BIRTH.` · `MAHAPAJAPATI STEPS IN.` · `SHE NURSED HIM HERSELF.` · `ANANDA SPEAKS FOR HER.` · then, large: `LOVE CAN BE ADOPTED.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let the breath settle. Then think of someone who raised you, or part of you. A parent, a grandparent, a stepparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you. Anyone who did some of the raising, whether or not they had to. Picture their face. Thank them silently. If that relationship is complicated, that's okay: you can thank the part that helped, and leave the rest. The bell holds the time.
Seven days. Queen Maya died a week after the birth, and her sister Mahapajapati raised the child as her own.
Your line: love can be adopted. Today, notice someone caring for a child, an animal, or a person who isn't theirs by birth, and honor it quietly. Day twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 25 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE WHOSE AIM SUCCEEDS.`

howItsDone: Buddhists honor both Maya, the Buddha's mother, and Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised him; Mahapajapati is remembered as the first Buddhist nun, and Buddhist teaching stresses gratitude to parents and those who raise us.

fork.reveal: she hands her own son to nurses and nurses Siddhattha herself, raising him as her own. years later, a discourse remembers it.

original.note: Pali: Mahāpajāpatī; Gotamī is her clan name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha had a charmed royal childhood.
what it means: his mother died when he was a week old, and his aunt raised him as her own.

what a scholar hears: the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (MN 123) states the seven-day pattern; in the Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (MN 142) Ananda recalls that she nursed him; tradition remembers her as the first bhikkhuni.

sources.ref: Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 123): the mother dies seven days after the birth
Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 142): Ananda recalls Mahapajapati's care

notes: Maya's rebirth in Tusita heaven (MN 123) is given as 'a heaven'; the Buddha teaching his mother (in Tavatimsa, in the Abhidhamma tradition) is mentioned as 'one story'. Confirm framing.
Mahapajapati giving her son Nanda to nurses: from the commentaries (Nidanakatha / Theri Apadana); confirm.
Meaning of the name Mahapajapati in the original note ('great leader of many') is uncertain; a Keeper should confirm or remove.
Her role as the first nun is only hinted at ('she'll come back later on this path').

Editor review (days 20-37 pass): SERIOUS fixes. (1) In MN 142 it is Ananda, not the Buddha, who says Mahapajapati was his mother's sister, nurse and foster mother and nursed him; the teach, match, myth, fork, trapdoor and source now say so. (2) Maya's rebirth in Tusita is in MN 123 itself, not 'the later tradition'; corrected. (3) The hook called Asita's tears 'tears of joy', contradicting day 24 (he wept for himself). Also cut the unsourced 'not unusual for a royal house', 'changes the whole community forever', the 'it breaks your heart' line, and the uncertain gloss 'great leader of many'. Keeper: confirm the MN 142 speaker and that leaving out the Buddha's reply is fair.
